opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to put it is this: in language models there was a moment when people saw that if you just add more data, more compute, and more parameters, performance goes up along a smooth, predictable curve. That predictability changed everything. Investment, talent, and engineering effort could all line up behind one recipe. In embodied intelligence we haven't had that moment yet. We have impressive demos, but we don't have a curve we can trust.

There are a few reasons. The first and most obvious is data. Language models had the internet, a huge accumulated record of human writing that was basically free to collect. Robots have nothing like that. Physical interaction data has to be produced one episode at a time, through teleoperation, real deployments, or simulation, and each source has problems. Teleoperation is expensive and slow. Simulation is cheap, but there's still a gap between simulated physics and the real world, especially for contact-rich manipulation. Human videos are abundant, but they don't contain actions or forces in a form a robot can use directly. So the first bottleneck is that we don't yet have a data flywheel that grows by orders of magnitude.

The second reason is heterogeneity. Text is text. Robots differ in arms, grippers, sensors, control frequencies, and bodies. If data from one embodiment doesn't transfer well to another, you can't simply pool everything into one giant dataset the way people did with web text. Cross-embodiment learning has been making progress, but it hasn't become a solved, scalable recipe.

The third reason, and I think it gets underappreciated, is evaluation. In language you can run a benchmark overnight. In robotics, evaluating a policy means running it on real hardware, in real scenes, many times, and the results are noisy. If you can't measure progress cheaply and reliably, you can't even confirm whether you're on a scaling curve. A lot of what looks like scaling might just be variance, or overfitting to a lab setup.

So when I say embodied intelligence hasn't reached its scaling milestone, I mean we haven't yet shown, convincingly and repeatably, that putting in ten times more data and compute gives you a predictably more general and capable robot across tasks, environments, and bodies. Once that is demonstrated, I think the field will change very quickly, much like language did. Capital and engineering will converge, and the question will become how fast we can build the data infrastructure, not whether the approach works.

Personally, I'm optimistic, but I think the breakthrough is less likely to come from a single clever model architecture and more likely from whoever first builds a system that makes physical data collection scale: cheaper hardware, deployment in the real world that generates data as a by-product, and better ways to use human video and simulation. Whoever builds that flywheel is probably the one who finds the scaling law.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that embodied intelligence hasn't had its "GPT-3 moment" yet, and the reason is that we haven't actually proven scaling works the way it did for language.

In language, the recipe was clear: more internet text, bigger transformers, more compute, and the loss curve kept going down. Everyone saw the same curve and believed in it. In robotics, nobody has shown that curve convincingly. We don't have an equivalent of "the internet" for physical interaction. Teleoperation data is expensive, simulation has a reality gap, and video from YouTube doesn't come with action labels. So the first thing scaling-up means to me is answering the data question: what is the cheap, abundant signal that actually improves a robot's physical capability when you add more of it?

The second piece is generalization across embodiments and tasks. Right now a lot of impressive demos are still one robot, one lab, one task distribution. A real scaling milestone is when a model trained on, say, a hundred different robot platforms performs better on a new platform than a model trained on just that platform. That's the analogue of pretraining helping downstream tasks. There are early signs, with the RT-X style efforts and the VLA models, but the gains are still modest compared to what we saw in language.

Third, there's a hardware loop that language models never had to deal with. You can't just buy more GPUs and get more robot experience. You need thousands of robots running reliably in the real world, and the hardware itself has to be good enough that the data is worth collecting. So scaling in embodiment is really co-scaling three things: models, data, and physical fleets. Companies that can close that flywheel, where deployed robots generate data that trains better models that justify more deployment, are the ones that will hit the milestone first.

So when I say the milestone hasn't been reached, I mean concretely: no one has yet published a clean scaling law for physical capability, and no one has a deployed fleet large enough to generate the data volume that would test it. I'm optimistic it's a few years away rather than decades, but we're still at the stage of figuring out the recipe, not executing it.

astra-6.text:
I think the scaling-up milestone means reaching a point where adding more data, more compute, and more training reliably produces better capabilities—and those capabilities transfer to new tasks and environments.

For embodied intelligence, the challenge is that the whole loop runs through the physical world. A robot has to perceive, act, and deal with the consequences of its actions. So collecting more data isn’t enough by itself. We need to understand which data helps, how to learn across different tasks and robot bodies, and how to measure whether the system is actually becoming more general.

For me, the milestone would be moving from a robot that performs a carefully rehearsed task to one that can handle unfamiliar situations with very little additional training. And we would need to show that this improvement follows a repeatable pattern as we increase scale. That’s what would make scaling a dependable path forward.

r002.rationale: It describes the milestone as reliably improving capabilities by adding data and compute, with improvement continuing as scale increases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the milestone is when adding more data, compute, and training reliably produces more capable robots. We’ve seen that pattern in language models, but embodied intelligence hasn’t yet demonstrated it as clearly.

A robot can do very well on a carefully prepared task, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the same approach will improve steadily across different objects, environments, and robot bodies. The real question is whether experience can accumulate into a general capability, rather than each new task requiring another round of engineering.

Part of the challenge is the data loop. A robot has to act in the physical world, gather useful feedback, and learn from failures. That makes collecting experience slower and more expensive, and it raises the question of how much learning can transfer from simulation or other robots.

So I wouldn’t define the milestone as a spectacular demonstration or a particular number of robots deployed. I’d look for a repeatable trend: as we scale training, success rates improve, unfamiliar tasks become easier to learn, and the amount of human intervention falls. Once that relationship becomes predictable, we’ll have a much stronger basis for saying embodied intelligence has reached its scaling-up stage.

r002.rationale: It describes the missing milestone as a predictable regime where scaling data and compute reliably makes robots more capable, which communicates continued improvement with scale.
